messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] MRDS graphs in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thibault, listfolk,

There isn't an "easy" way to extract this data from the plotting code at
the moment. So the easiest thing to do is to delve into the plot.* code
and try to pull out what you want. Find the corresponding plot file
(e.g. plot.io.R) then it's a case of working out what plot_cond and
plot_uncond will give you, then hack them to return the requisite
data.frames.

A while ago I wrote up how the different parts of the code work and how
they relate to the mathematical quantities in the literature, which may
be useful. You can find that information here:

http://distancedevelopment.github.io/mrds-Plotting.html

If you get somewhere with this then I'd be interested in including it in
mrds. If you have particular issues, feel free to contact me off list.

I hope this is helpful.

best,
--dave

messages.subject: Re: MRDS vs. CDS
messages.body_plain:
Problem was solved! Had to do with making sure both engines were running the same exact detection function.

On Thursday, January 29, 2015 at 2:28:36 PM UTC-6, Mary Annala wrote:
> Hello Distance Sampling Community:
> We seem to have come across some confusing data with our research project.  We are performing double-observer distance sampling aerial surveys for large mammals.  We have completed three sets of surveys so far and have ran the data through Distance (MRDS engine).  We took the data and ran it as conventional distance sampling (CDS  engine) so that we could compare the two techniques. We had fully expected for the CDS data to be lower than the MRDS data. However, our CDS values are much higher than our MRDS values. The CDS values are accompanied by higher CV's and wider confidence intervals.  We suspect the problem may be some sort of availability bias.  However, we haven't found solid evidence to prove or disprove this yet.  Does anyone have any insight as to what our potential problem could be? Is there an answer to why our CDS values are higher when it is expected for them to be lower than the MRDS values?
> Any help would be greatly appreciated!!
>
messages.body_snippet:
Problem was solved! Had to do with making sure both engines were running the same exact detection function.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Data binning to infinity
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

For binned data you need start and end points for each bin. These must be defined in the data filter for binned data. (The bin options in the model definition are purely for diagnostic purposes). The values of the datapoints within the bin is not important as it is actually anasyed in bins but usually people do use the mid point as you have suggested.

Your last bin is going to be problematic. Usually a bin with no end point would be excluded from the analyses, there is no way to specify an infinite end point (doing this would result in a bin of 0 height any way). Survey protocol may include one on the record sheet so that observers don't feel the need to heap observations just beyond a truncation distance into the final bin (which would cause analysis issues) but this bin would not be used for the analyses.

Laura

Dr. L. Marshall
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews

messages.subject: Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am looking at using distance sampling of scats: the scats are collected along line transects (usually 1km), and extracted DNA is used to identify individuals and therefore "recaptures", between and within transects - thus preventing repeated counts of the same individuals. We are able to extract viable DNA from about 30-40% of collected samples. We are confirming DNA degradation rates in scats experimentally and suspect it is about 3 weeks. Is this design (ie incorporating the scat "recaptures") possible using a distance sampling analysis, and if so, any advice or initial pointers in the right direction for information would help me a lot...

Regards,
Martin.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin & list

I’m not sure if it’s been tried, but what if for every individual on a transect you divided by the number of scats it produced and used that value in the cluster size column.  So if there were three records of an individual on the transect the ‘cluster size’ (effectively a multiplier) for the three entries for that individual would be 0.33.

I’m not sure what effect that would have on the variance - it might be useful to check section 2.1.4 of the distance book to see what it says about independence of samples.

You would probably have to ignore scats that were unable to be identified as they would not be accounted for in this method.  But it has the advantage that it might sidestep the need to know exactly what the lifespan of the scats was because that would be included in the probability of detection.

Roy had a thought that you could use SECR which might be able to extract more from the recapture information.

Cheers

Stewart

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
messages.body_plain:
I agree that secr is well worth considering.  But if you're going to use distance sampling, I would not be concerned about how many animals were sampled.  Instead, I would use indirect methods:  treat the scats themselves as the individuals, and estimate scat density.  To convert this to animal density, you would need to estimate the average number of scats an animal produces a day, and the mean time to decay of a scat.  Trying to convert sampled scats to number of animals detected will not work in a distance sampling context, because movement of animals over the period that the scats are available for detection will cause bias, and there is no guarantee that an animal 'on the line' will be detected by this means.  secr can use this additional information though.

Steve Buckland

Problem reading data file

C:\users\usuario\Documents\Guanaco\testy.txt

messages.subject: Bird surveys
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am just wondering whether Distance will be suitable for a particular study I am doing. I am looking at bird diversity and abundance on a farm that has a winter bird seed crop planted on it to aid bird conservation. I am looking at how birds use this crop into the winter. So I am doing weekly bird surveys which take into account what species were there and in what numbers. This is done in line with crop surveys to measure the dried weight of seeds per meter squared. So my question is, will distance allow me to enter data for more then one species at a time and will it let me do multiple weeks so that I can look at how the usage is changing throughout the winter. I would like to statistically test this and compare the different weeks etc etc.

Many thanks

Jay

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Bird surveys
messages.body_plain:
Jay:

The direct answer to your two questions are:

- can I enter data for more than a single species:  yes, create a field in the observation layer for species, then for each detection record the species
- can I 'do' multiple weeks: yes, you could think about treating weeks as strata

The Distance project "songbird" that is distributed with Distance as a sample project is likely closest to your situation.  That project has multiple species recorded (see "Species" field in Observation layer).  Data were gathered in 4 pastures across 2 years; consequently there are 8 strata, names 1980_x, where x is pasture number.  This example is in the Illustrative Examples Chapter of the Introduction to Distance Sampling Book, section 8.7. The data was gathered during an extensive survey of songbirds in the Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge in Colorado (Knopf et al. 1988).  The data are for two years and 4 pastures, and include multiple species.  Further details are in the Introduction to Distance Sampling book, or the original paper (Knopf et al. 1988. JWM 52:280-290).

You can produce stratum-specific estimates (by species, assuming sufficient numbers of sightings and transects) to make your statistical comparisons.  See Section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001) for formulae to compare density estimates.

messages.subject: Post-stratify and Multiplier
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

There are two things I would like to do in R and I'm wondering if "Distance libraries" can do that.
I already know how to do that in the distance software but I would like to be able to run all my analysis with R.

The first thing is including post-stratification when estimate the density (and abundance). I use the following characteristics in the "estimate" tab in the "model   definition" window of the Distance software:
Post-stratify using:
Layer type: Sample
Field name: Year
Sample def: Sample
Quantities to estimate and level of resolution:
Global(Density, Encounter rate and Cluster size)
Stratum(Density and Encounter rate)
Global density estimate: Mean (weighted by Total effort in stratum)

I want to calculate annual abundance using the detection function and cluster size both fitted over all years.

Can I do the same in R?

The other question is if I can apply a multiplier also in R (I do that in Distance using the Multipliers tab of the model definition window)

Any advice is welcome.
Thank you!

messages.subject: Adjusted angle zig zag error
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am having an issue that has been raised a couple of times on this forum over the  years.  I’m investigating a few different designs for a program we’re involved in, and the equal-angle and equal-spaced zig zag designs both run fine.  When I try an adjusted angle zig zag, however, I get multiple errors of the following type, and no results:

**Error: Problems generating the adjusted angle zigzag sampler. Too little effort for the survey region height of XXX

I am running Distance 6.2.  I have tried solving the problem – as prompted by Distance – by increasing the survey effort and adjusting the angle (there is only one stratum).

For some background, this is what I found: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/distance-sampling/too$20little$20effort$20for$20the$20survey$20region/distance-sampling/pc0eHrDlNGc/OJcSBbIur-8J

Like Philippe, I note that a design layer is created (despite not showing in the results) and I’m able to add it to a map.  However, I’m not able to estimate probability of coverage using the design (it generates the same errors).

Any ideas?

Stewart

messages.body_plain:
Stewart:

Thanks for digging back into the email list archives before writing to the list.  I am afraid we have not made any progress on the adjusted angle sawtooth design bug in the Survey Design Engine since the earlier report from 2010.  You'll need to content yourself with designs produced by the equal-spaced sawtooth (that has better properties than the equal-angle sawtooth).
